Honestly, crucially underrated game. One of the most fun games i've played in a decade, but you need at least one other friend who's as much into it as you are, and more people really expands your possibilities exponentially. This is not a single player horror game but a strictly multiplayer game where you roleplay as a content creator making vlogs, skits, documentaries and such. It's like playing chess alone, you technically can and i'm sure at least one person enjoys that, but you're not playing the game without someone else. 

The whole point is to mess around and have a laugh, and damn is the game so finely tailored for the chaos needed to make it happen. Admittedly it's on the niche side, but this game really helped me re-learn how to have fun with video games, rather than taking them too seriously. You have to go with the flow and not take it seriously.

As much as i like lethal company as a horror game conceptually (dungeon exploration/looting with intricate tools and numerous interesting entities alongside asymmetrical co-op gameplay), it's more funny than scary, even though it'll catch you offguard at times, just like content warning. But i've had so much more fun playing content warning. It's just way more masterfully crafted to do what it wants, and it knows what it wants. Many people miss the point and expect the game to give you the gameplay. This game is very different, YOU make the gameplay, if you are not creative and willing to make up scenarios, pretend play, roleplay a character/vlogger, or try to set up comedic moments, it will just simply not speak to you. In a way it is very sandbox-ey.

One of the big things that makes content warning so much better than lethal company, is that horror games are designed to play in the most boring, slow and cautious way possible especially if you want to optimize performance, which most survival horror games fail to make interesting. This game on the other hand encourages you to take as much risk as possible, and lets you get quite creative with it. The physics and ragdolls are so chaotic and flimsy, it leads to hilarious results, which comes with very satisfying tools to use as well, further adding to said chaos. 

The camera is a bit low on battery, and has a really poor range. It also cuts off too fast when you let go of it (i wish we could put it down and let it record a bit, or have a tripod), but the restriction actually creates on its own really funny cuts in the footage, comedic timing just happens on its own half the time. But you can also just record yourself doing stupid shit.

Whether you're just messing around in the hub, trying to do something fancy in the "dungeon", or rewatching the footage that you recorded, you're bound to have a good laugh with you friends. More maps/entities/tools/unlocks would be welcome.

Main issue is the game's wonkiness goes a bit far into the gamebreaking bugs territory, which can be annoying, the game isn't exactly stable.

Content Warning is a 10/10 game. I played a lot of games in a similar genre and assumed I wouldn't like this one either but good lord was I wrong. This game is in the same genre as lethal company but it is not the same game in the slightest. In no other game have I gone from cowering in a box to RUSHING FULL SPEED into death purely because I know we would make more money if I distracted the centipede demon for 10 seconds. That 8$ hospital bill was absolutely destroyed by the 241$ we made because of my sacrifice. 
I paid half price for this game, I wasn't lucky enough to get it free. That said I absolutely love it, please give it a try if you've got friends to play with.

1. Main complaint, only one person gets the camera, so only one person REALLY is in control of how well you do, leading the others to feel sort of useless.   The film in the camera is limited per run, so if you start to "have fun" by larping as a reporter or film team, you blow through the film too quickly and end up failing the objective.  Metagaming the objective by doing short clips of each scoring thing makes for a boring film and the rest of the players basically useless, its a single player experience masquerading as multiplayer.

2. A lot of the monsters it feels like there is little to no counterplay, other than "Avoid", which feels cheap and unfun especially when their patrol routes block your only way in

3. The difficulty is weird.  With each passing day the numbers get bigger, but the "View" scaling seems to scale just as linearly as the objective, so really you do the exact same thing over and over without it actually getting harder, unless you get RNG'd into a bad enemy spawn point

If you want to go more the lethal company route, give the other players some way to actually contribute to the objective other than just being backup camera holders after the main one dies.

The first session was genuinely fun. The second session was less fun. By the fifth session I was experiencing the specific kind of boredom that only comes from a game that peaked on the very first day you played it and had nowhere left to go.

Let me be upfront about one thing before I say anything critical. Content Warning was made in about two months by a team of five people at Landfall as an April Fools release, launched free for its first twenty-four hours, and attracted 6.6 million people to claim it on day one. For what it is, a small team's rapidly developed party game built around a clever social concept, that is an extraordinary achievement and I do not want to dismiss it. What I am going to discuss is whether that clever social concept has enough substance underneath it to hold up past the initial viral energy, and my honest answer is that for me it did not.

The pitch is genuinely charming. You and up to three friends descend into a creepy underground world called the Old World to film monsters and spooky events on a camera, then surface, upload the footage to a fictional platform called SpöökTube, and try to hit a view count quota to progress. The goal is to go viral. The monsters you film, the dangerous situations you get into, the screaming and the running and the chaotic deaths, all of it becomes content. The game is explicitly a comedy about social media and the pursuit of clout through manufactured danger, and that idea is smart and timely and had me laughing out loud during my first session as my friend got grabbed by something while I kept filming because we needed the views.

The problem is that this idea, which is funny, is also essentially the entire game. And while an idea can carry a first session on pure novelty and social comedy, it cannot carry a tenth session when the underlying gameplay loop is thin enough that you can see clean through it.

The Old World environments are procedurally generated but the rooms and corridors and the general visual aesthetic of them do not vary enough to feel genuinely different from run to run. After a few sessions you have seen everything the underground spaces have to offer and the discovery element that makes the early runs interesting is gone. The monsters are numerous but the way you interact with them is almost always the same: you try to film them, something goes wrong, somebody dies or nearly dies, you retrieve the camera and get out. The equipment progression gives you better gear to bring into the Old World but it does not meaningfully change how those runs feel in a way that compounds into a new layer of experience. You are doing the same thing but with a slightly better flashlight.

The social comedy carries the experience and when it is working it is genuinely funny. The problem is that the social comedy is dependent on the people you are playing with more than on the game itself. A group of four friends who are naturally funny and reactive and performative will have a great time with Content Warning regardless of what the game underneath is doing, because they are essentially creating their own entertainment and using the game as a backdrop. A group of people who are less naturally charismatic or who have played the game enough times that the situations feel familiar will find that the game does not generate the laughs on its own. The game is not the entertainment. The game is the container that your friends bring the entertainment to. When your friends are funny and fresh to the experience that container works great. When they have played it a dozen times and the monster appearances stop being surprising, the container starts feeling pretty empty.

The view count quota system that creates the game's progression tension also creates a particular kind of frustration that dulls over time. Losing a run and having to start the quota over with nothing to show for it is the designed consequence of failure but it compounds the repetition problem by sending you back to runs that already feel familiar rather than escalating toward something new. The progression feels like it is treading water rather than building toward anywhere.

I want to be careful not to hold a two-month April Fools project to the standards of a game designed with a full development cycle and serious content ambitions. Measured against what it is, Content Warning is a clever and charming party game with a great core joke that punches above its weight class during that initial window. Measured against whether I would recommend spending time and money on it past that window, I would not. It burns bright and brief and the people who had the most fun with it were the ones who played it when everyone was playing it together and the social energy of the moment was part of the experience.

That moment has passed. The game that remains without it is thin.

NOT RECOMMENDED.

Let it be known I do not post this review with malice, it is merely my opinion and I do believe this game can become something great in the future.

The main flaws:
It gets old quick
The art style (specifically of the below)
Luck based

I think the idea of the world is really good! A bright bubbly floating island with the old world below covered in, what I assume is, rot and full of monsters; What's not to love? But this falls apart when you go to the below world and realise that practically everything down there is the same UV map, and it is ridiculously hard to navigate. With everything looking the same I have gotten lost countless times, to the point I don't even want to explore deeper.
Secondly, it gets old and boring fast. Only a few runs in did I understood the gimmick, which was good, but if you're not a content creator yourself and just the average joe you may find this experience a bit less engaging. Watching youtubers play this, they clearly were having far more fun and I was overjoyed by that. Clearly, this game has an audience, I just may not be that audience.
Thirdly, there is so much luck involved. Sometimes you get a million monsters, sometimes you get one shot instantly and lose everything. Sometimes it takes ages and you only get a snail. I don't know if this is just my experience, but it makes it a lot harder to continue reaching the view count quota with this issue.

I think the monsters are really cool, ranging from stupid looking like the mixer to really creepy, like the grabby hand explosive guy. The only real thing is, they all have the same skin! It's so dull! I understand the purpose of this, but I really think it'd help make them more memorable if they had some variations!

I do think this game has a good sense of humour though, the character designs and changeable face plates are super fun and makes the group stand out against the dreary place below. The equipment, especially the sound maker personally, are super fun! 
The group is encouraged to stick together because of one thing; the camera. Everyone wants to be on camera, and from my understanding the viewers like when they see everyone. But this limits exploration! You can't split up and have separate harrowing experiences, or when you do, they are left uncaptured which is really sad!

I think a great addition to the game would be a second camera: Half the film, double the risk. It would mean you could split up in groups of two and at the end there could be a compilation of the two sides making lots of opportunities for funny cutaways.
Another addition I think would improve this game is perhaps daily goals. Maybe after the first 3 days you start getting highlighted comments requesting to see specific things, and you can choose to act on them. For example, show off how a snail damages you, see a star barnacle thing, maybe catch an explosion live on camera. This would add an element of speed to the game as well as you rush to find the things these commenters want. Of course, if this was a feature, it'd have to be made possible and not just luck based.

Overall, I think this game as of right now is fun in the beginning but quickly grows boring. But if it updates and adds new features, it can become something incredible. I am holding onto that hope, and I wish the developers all the best. Even if I may not personally enjoy it all that much, I still see merit in this game, and in the fun others are having with it.

Also, it's bloody cheap, I can't be too picky can I?

This game is okay. The gameplay loop and premise is very fun. The art style is wonderful, but the shading on the monochrome makes enemies difficult to distinguish between. The video replay is hilarious and the comments are very responsive to what is said and filmed. 

However, this game desperately needs a balance patch. The main objective is to walk up to monsters and film them, but most monsters one or two-shot you. There are no invincibility frames and they deal physics damage on top of their normal damage. This game is lowkey a wiki game for the monster behaviors, but the wiki has no photos and poor descriptions. There are no weapons other than the shock stick, meaning you can never increase your opportunities to get close to monsters without dying. The rounds only last 2 minutes meaning you can't really explore the cool environments, and the camera runs out of film almost immediately.

This game feels like it's a beta for an AMAZING experience. But it needs either difficulty settings or a general balance patch.

It is quite difficult to summarize the significance this game has had on my own personal life. This game has contributed to countless life lasting memories for me and my friends. It has strengthened and broken so many bonds within my own personal life, yet it is so hard to explain. This is a game where you and your friends get to pursue your childhood dreams of one day becoming an influencer or streamer, and has provided me with the opportunity of a lifetime. You are able to crack jokes and make those around you laugh while you fight off spooky monsters. A significant task of this is managing how much tape you utilize when you record, which ensures every second of the final product is full to the brim with humor. The premise of this game is very decent, but if things stay the same it will not achieve even a fraction of success lethal company had. 

Taking the idea of funny lethal company clips and making those clips the main goal of the game is extremely clever game design, but it is also flawed in it's core. That's because all of those funny lethal company clips are funny only because they occured naturally, as a byproduct of the lethal company main gameplay loop. In this game, the clips ARE the main gameplay loop. Because of that critical difference, clips in this game feel extremely forced and unnatural, and only rarely produce any fun. 

It would be much better if we had some useful instruments or traps to make the monster interactions fun, but now we only have 2 boring stunning weapons that do nothing to actually entertain you. 

Additionally, this game suffers from complete absence of any meaningful lore. There is a generic colorful rainbow island you live on, and there is a scary dark city filled with monsters and rotating gears. That's all. No text messages to be found. No pieces of lore to uncover. No monster encyclopedia. Nothing. The worldbuilding simply does not exist in this game, and it makes the entire game even more meaningless. 

In conclusion we have a small game that revolves around a good basic idea that is unfortunately not developed and is not accompanied by other mechanics. It is completely fine for a free game (which it used to be for the first 24 hours), but for a price any higher than half a dollar this game just does not perform well enough. It isn't even marked as an early access game, though it completely is an early access game. Makes me wonder if the developers actually do not plan to release any new updates, or just wanted to trick people into thinking this game is a complete product.

Content Warning is an okay game that's trying to invent the genre of "lethal-likes", I suppose you could call it. Essentially: cooperative, multiplayer comedic horror. Like every other review will tell you, the concept is great, but dear lord -- the gameplay is barren, empty and uncreative, and thus, it's incredibly difficult to actually have those funny moments with friends.

Aside from enemies, you will find that there is basically nothing for you to play around with. All of the maps have essentially the same layout and very little in the way of interactables or hazards, so if you wanna have fun in the Old World, you're going to have to bring your own stuff. Lethal Company did this much better, because the gameplay loop revolved around collecting items that were inherently funny. Instead, Content Warning expects you and your friends to be funny on your own, which is surprisingly difficult to accomplish for most groups. No airhorns or jars of pickles.

In fact, the items this game DOES have are still boring to play with. Half a dozen types of flashlights, some stunning items, a clapper, microphones, and emotes that must be purchased for EACH INDIVIDUAL PLAYER. And they aren't cheap, either. Very rarely will you ever have a chance to stock up on anything. Where's my spray paint, or my questionable performance enhancing helium?

A lot of the game's systems embrace Lethal Company's "hardcore" aspect too, but fail to recognize that the gameplay suffers immensely because of it. A quota is in order, and you have to meet it every three days in order to maintain your progress. If you die, you drop your stuff. If everybody dies in the Old World, you lose your footage for that day. And on top of that, the game judges the camera footage you record based on variety, and variety alone. All of this serves to stifle player creativity; If you want to make funny inside jokes, you're going to pay with terrible video performance. If you're holding onto items, money is so tight that you're discouraged from killing yourself in a comedic fashion. And if everybody fails, you lose your funny recording. You don't even get to keep a copy of it for personal viewing, it's just gone forever.

So in other words: the game works against you having a funny time, even though that's what you bought into it for. Womp womp. Go play Lethal Company with OBS enabled and it's basically a better experience in every way possible.

[h1]Go film something terrifying! [/h1]
Welcome to Content Warning, a four-player co-op horror game where you and your friends play as a group of struggling influencers. But does it really have to stay that way?

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
In Content Warning, you have one goal: become famous. Team up with your friends to film the craziest, funniest, and most terrifying videos you can to rack up views and followers. Oh... and try to stay alive. But that's really just a minor detail. After all, only one of you has to make it back with the camera. Not everyone. Why die, you ask? Because the funniest videos usually involve one or two of your friends meeting a horrible end.

Fall into a bottomless pit. Eat a bomb. Get chased down by one of the dozens of horrifying monsters lurking in the darkness and let it turn you into lunch. Just make sure someone keeps the camera rolling!

[h1]Final words[/h1]
If you're looking for a hilarious co-op horror game with proximity voice chat, plenty of laughs, a few genuine scares, and randomly generated maps that are anything but empty, Content Warning is an easy recommendation.

So grab three friends, hit record... and try to go viral before you become the content yourselves.

Cheers.
